title: Understanding neutrinos: The research that led to the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
excerpt: Physicist Francis Halzen was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to IceCube.
content:
Neutrinos are electrically neutral subatomic particles with extremely small masses that interact very weakly with matter. Produced by nuclear processes and high-energy astrophysical phenomena, they travel vast distances and carry information about some of the most extreme environments in the universe.

IceCube is a neutrino observatory located near the South Pole. The detector uses approximately one cubic kilometer of ice equipped with thousands of optical sensors to record the light produced when neutrinos interact with matter.

In 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen for his contributions to the development of IceCube and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. His work helped establish neutrino astronomy as a new way to study the universe.

What are neutrinos?

Neutrinos are elementary particles belonging to the lepton family, like electrons, but they have no electric charge and an extremely small mass. They interact through the weak nuclear force and gravity, making collisions with other particles extremely rare.

Trillions of neutrinos pass through the human body every second without producing any noticeable effects. These properties allow them to travel enormous distances across the universe without being absorbed or deflected.

These particles are produced through processes such as nuclear reactions inside stars, radioactive decay, supernova explosions, and interactions between cosmic rays and Earth's atmosphere. There are three types, or flavors, of neutrinos: electron, muon, and tau.

The IceCube Observatory

The IceCube Observatory is a neutrino detector located in Antarctica that uses one cubic kilometer of ice as its detection medium. Its structure contains thousands of optical sensors capable of recording light produced by secondary particles generated when a neutrino interacts with the ice.

Detecting neutrinos is difficult because they have no electric charge and interact with matter through the weak nuclear force. When a neutrino interacts with an atomic nucleus in the ice, it can produce charged particles that emit Cherenkov radiation, a bluish light recorded by the sensors.

How does IceCube work?

The IceCube Observatory has more than 5,000 sensors installed along 86 vertical strings, at depths ranging from approximately 1,450 to 2,450 meters (4,760 to 8,040 feet). When neutrinos interact with matter, they can generate charged particles. The resulting bluish light is captured by sensors that record its timing and intensity.

By analyzing the timing and spatial distribution of the detected light, researchers reconstruct the paths of secondary particles and estimate the direction and energy of the original neutrino. The observatory also detects particle cascades produced by other types of interactions.

2026 Nobel Prize in Physics

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to physicist Francis Halzen for his contributions to the IceCube Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. Halzen played a key role in turning Antarctic ice into a particle detector.

Unlike many recent years, when the prize was shared by two or three researchers, Halzen was the sole recipient of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. The award recognizes his scientific contributions, although IceCube itself is the result of an international collaboration.
